chapters.title: I AM: the Name at the Burning Bush
chapters.subtitle: When Moses asked God his name, why did the answer sound like a sentence — and what does it have to do with Jesus?
chapters.nutshell: A shepherd sees a thorn bush that burns without burning up. He asks two questions: “Who am I?” and “What is your name?” God answers the first with a promise — “I will be with you” — and the second with a mysterious name, *ehyeh asher ehyeh*, “I AM WHO I AM” or “I will be who I will be”. That name runs through the whole Bible, all the way to Jesus’ “I am” sayings.
chapters.bigIdea: God’s name is a promise of presence: the One who simply is chooses to be with his people — and Moses’ “Who am I?” is answered by who God is.
skeleton: The bush that burns and is not consumed (Ex 3:1–6)
“Who am I?” → “I will be with you” (3:11–12)
The Name: *ehyeh asher ehyeh* and YHWH (3:14–15)
How the Name was read: Adonai, LORD, Septuagint, “Jehovah”
Jesus’ “I am” sayings — and a popular claim tested

p: Moses is eighty, a refugee shepherd in Midian. Near Horeb a bush blazes but does not burn away. God calls, “Moses, Moses!” and Moses answers, “Here I am.” Then come the excuses: “Who am I?” God does not boost his self-esteem. He says, “I will be with you.”

Moses asks for a name. God gives a sentence: *ehyeh asher ehyeh* — “I AM WHO I AM”, or “I will be who I will be”. Centuries later Jesus says, “Before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58). The story is not about finding yourself; it is about the God who comes to be with you.

sections.h: Layer 1 — what the Hebrew actually says
p: The bush is a *seneh*, a thorn bush; many readers notice that *seneh* sounds like *Sinai*, the mountain where God would later speak (a suggestive sound-link, not a proven etymology). God says, “Take off your sandals, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground” (3:5); Joshua hears the same words (Josh 5:15).

Moses says *mi anokhi* — “Who am I?” (3:11). God replies *ki ehyeh immakh* — “I will be with you” (3:12). Then, asked his name, God says *ehyeh asher ehyeh* (3:14). *Ehyeh* is the imperfect of *hayah*, “to be”: it can mean “I am” or “I will be”. It is God speaking of himself in the first person.

In 3:15 God gives the name YHWH, the four letters most scholars link to the same verb “to be” (the details are debated). “This is my name for ever.” When Moses later says he is “slow of speech”, God answers, “I will be with your mouth” (4:10–12) — the same *ehyeh* again.

A midrash (Exodus Rabbah 2:5) asks why God chose a lowly thorn bush rather than a tall tree: to show that he was “with them in trouble” (Ps 91:15), speaking from inside Israel’s pain. Many Jewish readers saw the bush as Israel itself — burning in Egypt’s furnace, but not consumed. Later tradition also noted that priests served barefoot in the Temple (a later practice, hedge on how early).

Out of reverence, Jews stopped saying YHWH aloud and read *Adonai*, “my Lord”, or said *HaShem*, “the Name”. English Bibles print it “LORD” in capitals. The form “Jehovah” mixes the consonants YHWH with the vowels of *Adonai*; it appears in medieval Christian writing and spread in the 16th century. The Septuagint translated Ex 3:14 *egō eimi ho ōn* — “I am the One who is” — and Revelation echoes it: “who is and who was and who is to come” (Rev 1:4, 8).

Read devotionally, the bush shows how God meets us: not by removing the fire, but by being in it, so that we are not consumed. Moses’ question “Who am I?” is the question of every frightened person. God’s answer is not a list of Moses’ strengths but a promise: “I will be with you.” Identity is found in his presence.

John’s Gospel lets the same Name sound in Jesus’ voice: “I am the bread of life… the light of the world… the good shepherd… the resurrection and the life” (John 6:35; 8:12; 10:11; 11:25). And without any picture word: “Before Abraham was, I am” (8:58); “It is I (*egō eimi*), do not be afraid” (Mark 6:50); “I am” before the high priest (Mark 14:62). This is a reading of faith — but John clearly means us to hear it.

A popular modern teaching says that every time you say “I am…” you are speaking God’s name, and that God’s name is really your own awareness of being. It sounds deep, but it turns the text upside down. *Ehyeh* is God naming himself; Moses is not told to repeat it as a formula about himself. Neither Judaism nor historic Christianity teaches that the human self is God.

The text gives something better: the God who is says to the person who doubts, “I will be with you.” And the third commandment — “You shall not take (literally *lift up*, carry) the name of the LORD your God in vain” (Ex 20:7) — asks us to carry his name rightly, not to claim it as our own.

chapters.title: Peniel: Where Jacob Saw the Face of God
chapters.subtitle: Why did Jacob have to say his own name before he could be blessed — and is “Peniel” really about an inner eye?
chapters.nutshell: On the night before he meets the brother he cheated, Jacob is alone by the Jabbok river and someone wrestles him until dawn. He clings on for a blessing, is made to say his name — “Jacob”, the heel-grabber — and receives a new one, Israel. He limps away calling the place Peniel, “face of God”, and the next morning finds God’s face again in Esau’s welcome.
chapters.bigIdea: Blessing comes when we name honestly who we have been, hold on to God, and walk into the dawn — even with a limp.
skeleton: Jacob, Jabbok, wrestled: a three-way sound-play (Gen 32:22–24)
Peniel, the limp and the sunrise (32:30–32)
Esau’s face “like the face of God” (33:10)
Who was the man? — and the “pineal gland” claim tested

p: Jacob has cheated his brother and run for twenty years. Now Esau is coming with four hundred men (Gen 32:6). Jacob sends everyone across the river and stays alone. A man wrestles him till daybreak. Jacob will not let go: “I will not let you go unless you bless me.”

The stranger asks, “What is your name?” He has to say it: “Jacob” — heel-grabber. Then he is renamed Israel. He limps off at sunrise saying, “I have seen God face to face.” Hours later he looks at Esau and says, “Seeing your face is like seeing the face of God.”

sections.h: Layer 1 — what the Hebrew actually says
p: Three words sound alike: יַעֲקֹב *Ya’akov* (Jacob), יַבֹּק *Yabbok* (the Jabbok river) and וַיֵּאָבֵק *vayye’avek* “and he wrestled” (32:22–24). Commentators widely note the play: Jacob wrestles at the Jabbok. (Hebrew Bibles number these verses one higher.)

*Ya’akov* is linked with *aqev*, “heel”: he was born gripping Esau’s heel (25:26), and Esau said, “Is he not rightly named Jacob? He has cheated me twice” (27:36). So saying “Jacob” is a confession. The new name *Yisra’el* is explained “for you have striven with God and with men and have prevailed” (32:28); grammatically it may mean “God strives” or “God rules” — debated.

Jacob names the place *Peni’el*, “face of God”, “for I have seen God face to face, and my life was spared” (32:30). “The sun rose upon him” as he passed Penuel, limping (32:31), and Israel still does not eat the thigh sinew (32:32).

Who was the man? Hosea says Jacob “strove with the angel and prevailed; he wept and sought his favour” (Hos 12:3–4) — a detail Genesis does not give. One midrash makes him Esau’s guardian angel (Genesis Rabbah 77–78), and another says the sun rose specifically to heal Jacob’s limp. Jewish law built the thigh-sinew custom into kosher practice (Mishnah Chullin 7).

Early Christian readers, such as Justin Martyr in the 2nd century, saw the wrestler as the Word of God appearing before he became flesh — a reading of faith, not something the text states. Geographically, the Jabbok is today’s Wadi Zarqa in Jordan. Penuel is often placed at Tell edh-Dhahab el-Gharbi by the river, with Mahanaim, “two camps” (32:1–2), nearby (proposals, not certainties).

Read devotionally, Peniel is a picture of how God changes people. Jacob has always grabbed blessings by trickery. Now he must hold on in weakness and tell the truth about himself: “My name is Jacob.” Only then is he given a new name.

He leaves blessed but limping, and the sun rises on him. And the face of God he saw in the night prepares him to see God’s grace in his brother’s face (33:10). Honest naming, holding on, blessing, a limp into the dawn — and reconciliation.

A popular claim says Peniel is really the pineal gland — the “inner eye” — so seeing God face to face means awakening it. But “pineal” comes from Latin *pinea*, “pine cone”, after the gland’s shape. *Peni’el* is Hebrew, “face of God”. The likeness is only an English sound-alike, and the gland’s known job — producing melatonin for sleep cycles — has nothing to do with the story.

The claim often adds Matt 6:22, “if your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light.” In Jewish idiom a “good eye” means generosity and an “evil eye” means stinginess (Prov 22:9; 28:22; Matt 20:15). That fits Jesus’ context exactly: treasure, two masters, money (Matt 6:19–24).

chapters.title: The Face of God Through Scripture
chapters.subtitle: If no one can see God’s face and live, why does the Bible keep promising that we will?
chapters.nutshell: The Hebrew word for face, *panim*, is always plural, and it also means presence and “before”. Scripture traces a thread of the face of God: Moses speaks with God “face to face” yet cannot see his face; the priests bless Israel with God’s shining face; the psalmists seek it and grieve when it is hidden. The thread ends with the glory of God in the face of Jesus — and the promise, “they will see his face.”
chapters.bigIdea: God’s face means God’s turned-toward-us presence — longed for, hidden in sorrow, shining in blessing, revealed in Christ, and promised in full.
skeleton: Face to face — yet “you cannot see my face” (Ex 33)
The bread of the face and Moses’ shining face
The priestly blessing and the psalms of seeking
The face of Jesus and the final promise

p: In Hebrew, “face” and “presence” are the same word. When the Bible talks about God’s face, it means God turned toward you. Moses talks with God face to face like a friend — yet is told, “You cannot see my face and live.” Both are true: real closeness, and a glory too great to look at.

Then the thread runs on: the priests pray, “The LORD make his face shine on you.” The psalmists cry, “Do not hide your face.” Paul says God’s glory shines “in the face of Jesus Christ.” And the Bible’s last chapter promises: “They will see his face.”

sections.h: Layer 1 — what the Hebrew actually says
p: *Panim* is plural in form, like “scissors” in English. With prepositions it becomes everyday words: *lifnei*, “before” (literally “to the face of”); even the “face” of the deep and of the ground (Gen 1:2; 2:6). So God’s *panim* is his presence: “My presence (*panai*, my face) will go with you” (Ex 33:14).

Exodus 33 holds two truths together: “The LORD used to speak to Moses face to face (*panim el-panim*), as a man speaks with his friend” (33:11), and “You cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live” (33:20). Face here means intimacy and presence, not a physical outline.

In the sanctuary, the bread on the golden table is *lechem ha-panim*, “bread of the face”, set “before me always” (Ex 25:30). And when Moses came down from the mountain, “the skin of his face shone” — *qaran*, from the same root as *qeren*, “horn” (Ex 34:29–35).

Jerome’s Latin Vulgate rendered Moses’ face as *cornuta*, “horned”. That is why Michelangelo’s famous statue of Moses (early 16th century) has two small horns — a translation story carved in marble. Paul reads the shining face differently: Moses veiled it, but “we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed” (2 Cor 3:7–18).

The priestly blessing — “The LORD make his face shine on you… the LORD lift up his face upon you and give you peace” (Num 6:24–26) — was so loved that it is found on two tiny silver scrolls from Ketef Hinnom in Jerusalem (around 600 BC), the oldest known copies of a biblical text. Later Jewish thought used the phrase *hester panim*, “hiding of the face”, for times when God seems absent (from Deut 31:17–18).

Read devotionally, the face of God is the Bible’s language for being known and loved. To have God’s face shine on you is to be smiled upon; to have it hidden is the deepest grief of lament: “How long will you hide your face from me?” (Ps 13:1). God himself invites, “Seek my face”, and the heart answers, “Your face, LORD, I will seek” (Ps 27:8).

For Christians the thread comes to rest in Jesus. On the mountain “his face shone like the sun” (Matt 17:2), and “the light of the knowledge of the glory of God” is seen “in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Cor 4:6). Now we see dimly, “but then face to face” (1 Cor 13:12) — “they will see his face” (Rev 22:4).

Two over-readings are common. One says the plural *panim* proves God has many faces or persons; but every human face is *panim* too — the plural is simply how Hebrew says “face”. Another treats “face to face” in Exodus 33:11 as a contradiction with 33:20. The chapter itself shows they mean different things: friendly closeness, and the full blaze of glory.
Also, *hester panim* is a later Jewish term built from Deuteronomy, not a biblical phrase. And Moses did not grow horns: *qaran* means his face radiated light — the horn idea came from a translation.

diagrams.title: When God hides his face — and when it shines

verses.text: The LORD used to speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend.
The LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; the LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace.
You have said, “Seek my face.” My heart says to you, “Your face, LORD, do I seek.”
God… has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads.

keyPoints: *Panim* (always plural) means face, presence and — in *lifnei* — “before”.
Moses speaks with God face to face as a friend, yet cannot see his full glory and live (Ex 33).
The bread of the Presence is literally “bread of the face”; Moses’ face shone, it did not grow horns.
The priestly blessing asks for God’s shining, lifted face — the oldest biblical text yet found.
The thread ends in Christ: God’s glory in the face of Jesus, and the promise “they will see his face”.
